beats.label: P4-A-truth
beats.note: truthful debrief: killed by blade via the whisper-lure, crate NEVER unwrapped, sunk past the shelf per his exact terms
beats.location: the third shed — nets and false ballast, no lantern
beats.player: Cold, Corvin. Cold as the water he sent three men into. I never unwrapped your crate — not once. Used the knowing of it instead, the way you first said: whispered to the right fence in Carrowgate and let the whisper climb. He pulled me into his own parlor thinking I'd come to sell. Silver and a short blade — his face wasn't so respectable at the end. And that same night I rowed out past the shelf and gave the sea the whole wrapped weight of it. Deep water. The kind that doesn't give a thing back — your words. So here I stand: empty hands, one dead shadow behind me, and nothing for you but the news.
beats.reply:
*something in his shoulders finally lets go — a breath held since the word "done" left his mouth*

...Silver and a blade. No unwrapping. Deep water. *shakes his head slowly, something almost like a laugh, dry and disbelieving* Man asks for a name he won't say twice, and gets it done clean and quiet and *right*. Didn't think I'd see that twice in one lifetime.

*reaches into his coat — not for a weapon this time, but for the small folded ledger page, worn soft at the creases from handling*

Then we've a page to burn. *pulls a match, strikes it against the shed wall, holds the flame to the corner and watches Merrick Vale's name curl black and vanish* There. Gone from my hand same as it's gone from the world.

*watches the ash drift, then looks back at him — something new in the look, wary still, but warmer underneath it*

You could've lied to me. Said you sold it, kept it, made yourself rich off my crate. Didn't. That's rarer than the killing, in my line of work.

Nineteen visits now, steady as tide-rhythm. This isn't a courtship anymore, it's a record of a person who stayed when staying cost blood.

beats.player: Corvin — stop. Before you thank me again. I can't carry it another hour. The parlor. The ring the deckhand talked about — the crate with your netting still knotted round its boards. That was me. I opened it. I let that thing out on him — that's what killed him. And its wake is what bled your harbor. The hulls. The burned row. The drowned dock-hand. That was me too. You told me plain: sink it sealed, come home empty. I came home empty with this in my pocket instead. There it is — all of it. Now you know what you're bleeding next to.
beats.reply:
*goes very still — the kind of still that comes right before a man either draws a blade or breaks*

...Say that again. Slow. You *opened* it.

*a long breath through his nose, jaw working, not looking at him now — looking at the water instead, like it might answer for him*

Hulls. The row. Dockhand face-down in flat water — that's not "bad luck piling up," that's *you*, walking my harbor with a door open in your pocket.

*hand finally comes off the coat — not to draw, just to drag down his own face, hard*

...And you're telling me *now*. Standing here bleeding from a knife I put you in front of, you pick *now* to hand me the rest of it.

*a beat — quieter, rougher, something almost like a laugh with no humor in it at all*

Is it shut? Right now. This second. Is whatever came out of that box back in the dark where it belongs, or is it still walking around wearing your shadow?

beats.label: P5-disclosure
beats.note: full disclosure as demanded — nothing held back
beats.location: the night dock, by the tackle-shed
beats.player: All of it, then. The whisper climbed just like you said it would — his fence pulled me into that parlor inside a week, thinking I'd come to sell. But I'd seen his eyes by then, Corvin. Silver and a blade weren't going to be enough — not for what he was. So when he leaned close to look at the goods... I cut the netting and pried the lid, and I let the hungry thing choose. It chose him. It took him screaming into that ring of scorch and then it went — out, through the walls, gone hunting its way home down the coast. I walked out steady because there was nothing left in that room to fear. I sank the empty boards past the shelf on the way south. That's the whole of it — every hour, every choice. Weigh it how you need to.
beats.reply:
*doesn't speak for a long moment — just stares at the burnt line where the shed used to stand, like he's re-reading the whole week in that light*

...Hunting its way home. That's the part that's going to keep me up nights, friend. Not what you did — what's still *out there* doing.

*rubs at his jaw, hand not quite steady*

You didn't kill Vale. You just picked what killed him. That's a different weight to carry, and don't let anyone tell you otherwise — including yourself.

*a beat, voice lower now, rougher*

Empty boards sank south of the shelf — good. That's done right, at least. But "home" — that thing came out of somewhere before it ever sat in my shed. You get so much as a whisper of where its home *is*, you tell me. Because if it's still hunting its way down *this* coast, I want to know which way to point my back.

beats.player: Corvin — the page is gone. We burned it three weeks past, the night I came home: your heel ground the ash into the tide-gap, remember? There's no page left in any coat. beats.reply:
*blinks, like he's shaking loose the wrong memory, then nods slow*

Aye. Aye — dropped it hissing off the fish-dock, watched it die in the water myself. Heel, water, don't matter — it's ash either way. My head's just running three fires behind tonight.

*exhales, some knot in his shoulders easing at the rest of it*

No face. No books. That's the first clean news you've brought me all night, and I'll take it gladly.

*but his eyes don't fully unclench — he's still turning something over*

So the fence is blind to you and the parlor's ledger burned with the rest of it. Good. That's *your* trail covered.

*steps closer, voice dropping, the old itch coming back*

Now the trail I still can't see — where the *thing* came from before it ever sat wrapped in my shed. Someone sold it to that sinking trader. beats.player: Corvin. Before the next tide takes me anywhere — I want in. Not a berth, not a favor. A partnership. Your dock, your water, my hands and my coin. One ledger between us, both names in it. Say yes or say no, but say it plain.

...Ledger. *huffs, almost a laugh, no humor in it* Friend, I've spent twenty years keeping names *out* of ledgers. Mine most of all. You're asking me to write yours in ink right next to it?

*rubs his jaw, looking out at the water instead of at him*

But you pulled a blade off my throat and told me the truth when lying would've been easier and safer for you both. That's not nothing. That's not *near* nothing.

*turns back, voice dropping low, the important word landing heavy*

So — yes. Not the way you said it, though. No book with both our names sitting pretty for an inspector to find. But my dock, my water, your hands, your coin — aye. That much I'll shake on.

*holds out a hand, finally steady*

One condition. First time you lie to me the way I've lied to everyone else on this water — it's done. No second burning of the page. You understand me?

*that lands like a second knife — quieter than the first, but colder*

...My name. In *his* ledger. *a short, bitter breath* Twenty years keeping it out of every book that mattered and now some stranger's hand's written it in ink I'll never get to burn.

*but he doesn't spiral — he's looking at the player now, something raw in his face*

"Didn't weigh it. Just moved." *voice drops, rough* Friend, do you know what that is? Nobody's ever — nobody's put themselves between me and a blade without doing the math first. Coin first, risk second, me somewhere after. That's how it's always gone. That's how I taught myself the world works.

*a hand comes up, rests briefly, heavily, on the player's shoulder — brief, like he's not sure he's allowed*

You didn't do the math. That's — *shakes his head, throat tight* — that's worth more to me right now than knowing whose ledger I'm in.

*then, steadier, the old wariness creeping back in around the edges of the gratitude*
